To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the genetic correlation between residual feed intake and feed conversion ratio is positive, that the genetic correlation is negative for carcass dressing percent, that the genetic correlations between residual feed intake of growing pigs and meat quality traits are positive for carcass back fat thickness and ultimate pH and negative for meat color, and that the genetic correlation with lean content in the carcass is negative.
selection for low RFI has the potential to decrease feed intake, improve feed conversion ratio, and increase lean meat content of carcasses.

the heritability of residual feed intake is moderate (0.24 +/-0.03), that selection for low RFI has the potential to reduce feed conversion ratio and daily feed intake, that it will increase carcass fatness and decrease carcass lean meat and dressing percent, and that it will decrease ultimate pork pH and lightness.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a selection program aimed at improving feed efficiency in pigs.
the genetic control of feed efficiency in pigs, with emphasis given to residual feed intake as the criterion for selection.
genetic relationships between residual feed intake and other traits of interest for pig producers and consumers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

selection for low RFI in pigs is expected to result in a moderate improvement in feed conversion ratio with a slight reduction of daily feed intake and a slight decrease in carcass dressing percent, but at the cost of an increased fat content in the carcass, which may be compensated by a higher proportion of lean meat in the carcass.

selection for low RFI in Large White pigs is expected to increase growth performance and improve carcass composition and meat quality traits, with the possible exception of carcass dressing percent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
selection for low feed intake of pigs is a promising approach to reduce feed costs and to improve feed conversion, with minimal correlated response for growth rate.
genetic improvement in feed efficiency is possible without compromising the growth and carcass quality of growing pigs.

selection for low RFI in pigs having ad lib. access to feed should be expected to improve growth performance and reduce daily feed consumption with minimal correlated effect on ADG, but with some correlated effect on carcass and meat traits, which are of interest to the pork industry.
The main takeaway from our work is that
selection for low feed conversion ratio and daily feed intake is expected to improve carcass composition and pork quality.

selection for low feed intake in growing-finishing pigs is expected to improve feed efficiency and to reduce daily feed intake without major detrimental effects on growth, carcass and meat composition, and meat quality, but with a tendency to decrease carcass dressing percentage.

the genetic improvement of feed efficiency in pigs is possible with minimal negative correlated effects for growth and carcass composition traits and with a positive correlated effect for pork quality.
